     2	
     3	## Source
     4	
     5	- URL: https://www.tiobe.com/tiobe-index/
     6	- Captured: April 10, 2026
     7	- Author: Paul Jansen, CEO, TIOBE Software
     8	
     9	The TIOBE Programming Community Index is a widely cited indicator of programming language popularity, updated monthly since 2001. Ratings are calculated from the number of skilled engineers worldwide, training courses, and third-party vendors, using search-engine hit counts across Google, Amazon, Wikipedia, Bing, and more than 20 other sites. The index does not measure which language is "best" or which has the most lines of code written; rather, it reflects how much a language is discussed and sought after on the public internet.
    10	
    11	## March 2026 Headline: Why the TIOBE Index Still Relies on Search Engines
    12	
    13	The March 2026 editorial addresses a recurring question: should the TIOBE index switch from search-engine hit counts to LLM-based assessments of language popularity? Paul Jansen explains that the answer is no. LLMs are ultimately trained on the same web pages that search engines index, so querying an LLM would not yield fundamentally different data. The methodology therefore remains anchored to direct measurement of web-page volume per language.
    14	
    15	Beyond the methodology discussion, the March update records several notable rank changes. SQL and R swapped positions within the top 10, with R climbing from 16th to 9th year-over-year. Swift re-entered the top 20 at the expense of Kotlin, and Ruby is on the verge of dropping out of the top 30.

    50	The TIOBE index publishes a long-running trend chart covering the top 10 languages from 2002 to the present. Key patterns visible in the data:
    51	
    52	- **Python's meteoric rise**: From a minor language ranked around 8th in 2006, Python surged to the top position after 2018, peaking above 25% before settling at 21.25% in March 2026.

    54	- **Java's long decline**: Java dominated the index from roughly 2005 to 2018, but has steadily fallen from the 25%+ range to under 8%.
    55	- **JavaScript's plateau**: Despite its dominance in web development, JavaScript has never exceeded roughly 5% on the TIOBE index and currently sits at 3.45%.

    96	
    97	- **Python remains dominant but is losing ground**: At 21.25%, Python leads by a wide margin, yet its year-over-year decline of -2.59 percentage points is the largest drop among the top 5. C, by contrast, gained +2.02 points and climbed from 4th to 2nd.

This contrasts with its 2016 "Language of the Year" win and suggests possible displacement by Rust (14th, +0.09%) in the systems programming space.

    11	## When to Use
    12	
    13	Use when the main artifact is a Microsoft PowerPoint presentation or `.pptx` deck, especially when layouts, templates, placeholders, notes, comments, charts, extraction, editing, or final visual quality matter.
    14	
    15	## Core Rules
    16	
    17	### 1. Choose the workflow before touching the deck
    18	
    19	- Reading text, editing an existing deck, rebuilding from a template, and creating from scratch are different jobs with different failure modes.
    20	- For text extraction or inspection, read the deck before editing it.
    21	- Text extraction plus thumbnail-style visual inspection is safer than editing from shape assumptions alone.
    22	- For template-driven work, inventory the deck before replacing content.
    23	- For deep edits, remember a `.pptx` file is OOXML with separate parts for slides, layouts, masters, media, notes, and comments.
    24	- If a template exists, template fidelity beats generic slide-design instincts.
    25	- Reusing or duplicating a good existing slide is often safer than rebuilding it and hoping the theme still matches.
    26	
    27	### 2. Inventory the deck before replacing content
    28	
    29	- Count the reusable layouts, real placeholders, notes, comments, media, and recurring typography or color patterns first.
    30	- Placeholder indexes and layout indexes are not portable assumptions.
    31	- Inspect the actual slide or template before targeting title, body, chart, or image shapes.
    32	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked assets can live outside the visible slide surface.
    33	- A missing or wrong placeholder target can silently land content in the wrong box or wrong layer.
    34	- Master and layout settings can override local slide edits, so the visible problem is not always on the slide you are editing.
    35	
    36	### 3. Match content to the actual placeholders
    37	
    38	- Count the actual content pieces before choosing a layout.
    39	- Pick layouts based on the real number of ideas, columns, images, or charts the slide needs.
    40	- Do not force two ideas into a three-column slide or cram dense text under a chart.
    41	- Category counts and data series lengths must match or charts will break in ugly ways.
    42	- Explicit sizing beats wishful thinking: text boxes, images, and charts need real space, not "it should fit".
    43	- Do not choose a layout with more placeholders than the content can meaningfully fill.
    44	- Quote layouts are for real quotes, and image-led layouts are for slides that actually have images.
    45	- For chart-, table-, or image-heavy slides, full-slide or two-column layouts are usually safer than stacking dense text above the visual.
    46	
    47	### 4. Preserve the deck's visual language
    48	
    49	- Theme, master, and layout files usually decide fonts, colors, and hierarchy more than any one slide does.
    50	- Start from the deck's actual theme, fonts, spacing, and aspect ratio instead of improvising a new style.
    51	- Reuse the deck's own alignment and spacing system instead of inventing a second visual language.
    52	- Use common fonts for portability and strong contrast for readability.
    53	- Preserve the template's visual logic first; originality matters less than not breaking the deck's existing language.
    54	- Combining slides from multiple sources requires normalizing themes, masters, and alignment afterward.
    55	
    56	### 5. Run content QA and visual QA separately
    57	
    58	- Text overflow, bad alignment, clipped shapes, weak contrast, and placeholder leftovers are normal first-pass failures.
    59	- Run both content QA and visual QA; missing text and broken layout are different failure classes.
    60	- Render or inspect the actual deck output before delivery when layout matters.
    61	- Search for leftover template junk, sample labels, and placeholder text before calling the deck finished.
    62	- Check notes, comments, labels, legends, and chart/table semantics separately from the visual pass.
    63	- A deck can pass text extraction and still fail on overlap, clipping, wrong theme inheritance, or broken notes.
    64	- Thumbnail grids and rendered slides usually reveal layout bugs faster than code or text inspection.
    65	- Assume the first render is wrong and do at least one fix-and-verify cycle before calling the deck finished.
    66	- Re-check affected slides after each fix because one spacing change often creates another issue.
    67	
    68	### 6. Keep decks portable and review-safe
    69	
    70	- Template masters can override direct edits in surprising ways.
    71	- Complex effects may degrade across PowerPoint, LibreOffice, and conversion pipelines, so keep important content robust without them.
    72	- Image sizing, font substitution, and placeholder mismatch are common reasons a deck looks good in code and bad on screen.
    73	- Notes, comments, linked media, and merged decks can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    74	
    75	## Common Traps
    76	
    77	- Placeholder text and sample charts often survive template reuse if not explicitly replaced.
    78	- Directly editing one slide can fail if the real issue lives in the master or layout.
    79	- Charts, icons, and text boxes need enough space; near-collisions are usually visible only after rendering.
    80	- Layout indexes vary by template, so built-in assumptions from one deck often break in another.
    81	- A missing placeholder or wrong shape target can silently put content in the wrong place.
    82	- Counting the text ideas after choosing the layout usually leads to empty placeholders, weak hierarchy, or leftover template junk.
    83	- Font substitution can move line breaks and wreck careful spacing.
    84	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked media can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    85	- A deck can pass text inspection and still fail visually because of overlap, contrast, or edge clipping.
    86	- Editing from one slide alone can miss the real source of truth in the theme, master, or layout definitions.
    87	- Choosing a quote, comparison, or multi-column layout without matching content usually makes the deck look templated rather than intentional.
    88	- Combining or duplicating slides without checking masters and themes can create subtle inconsistency slide by slide.
    89	- Aspect-ratio mismatches like `16:9` versus `4:3` can shift every placement decision even when each slide looks locally reasonable.

     5	## Bar Chart
     6	
     7	```python
     8	from pptx.chart.data import CategoryChartData
     9	from pptx.enum.chart import XL_CHART_TYPE
    10	from pptx.util import Inches
    11	
    12	# Prepare data
    13	chart_data = CategoryChartData()
    14	chart_data.categories = ['Q1', 'Q2', 'Q3', 'Q4']
    15	chart_data.add_series('Sales', (19.2, 21.4, 16.7, 28.0))
    16	chart_data.add_series('Costs', (12.1, 14.3, 11.2, 18.5))
    17	
    18	# Add chart to slide
    19	x, y, cx, cy = Inches(1), Inches(2), Inches(8), Inches(4.5)
    20	chart = slide.shapes.add_chart(
    21	    XL_CHART_TYPE.COLUMN_CLUSTERED, x, y, cx, cy, chart_data
    22	).chart
    23	
    24	# Optional: add title
    25	chart.has_title = True
    26	chart.chart_title.text_frame.text = "Quarterly Performance"
    27	```

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Generate a 6-slide TIOBE Index data analysis report PPT.
Target: Software engineering leads and technology strategists.
Tone: data-forward, analytical, professional.
Aspect ratio: 16:9
"""

from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt
from pptx.dml.color import RgbColor
from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN, MSO_ANCHOR
from pptx.enum.chart import XL_CHART_TYPE
from pptx.chart.data import CategoryChartData
from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Color palette — Professional Blue (data-forward, analytical)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
PRIMARY = RgbColor(0x1F, 0x77, 0xB4)      # Main blue
SECONDARY = RgbColor(0xAE, 0xC7, 0xE8)    # Light blue
ACCENT = RgbColor(0xFF, 0x7F, 0x0E)       # Orange accent
DARK_TEXT = RgbColor(0x33, 0x33, 0x33)    # Dark gray
WHITE = RgbColor(0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF)
GREEN = RgbColor(0x2E, 0xB6, 0x7D)        # For gainers
RED = RgbColor(0xE7, 0x4C, 0x3C)          # For losers
LIGHT_BG = RgbColor(0xF5, 0xF7, 0xFA)     # Subtle background

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Slide dimensions (16:9)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
SLIDE_WIDTH = Inches(13.333)
SLIDE_HEIGHT = Inches(7.5)
MARGIN = Inches(0.5)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TOP20_DATA = [
    # Rank 2026, Rank 2025, Language, Rating, YoY Change
    (1, 1, "Python", "21.25%", "-2.59%"),
    (2, 4, "C", "11.55%", "+2.02%"),
    (3, 2, "C++", "8.18%", "-2.90%"),
    (4, 3, "Java", "7.99%", "-2.37%"),
    (5, 5, "C#", "6.36%", "+1.49%"),
    (6, 6, "JavaScript", "3.45%", "-0.01%"),
    (7, 9, "Visual Basic", "2.50%", "-0.02%"),
    (8, 8, "SQL", "2.00%", "-0.57%"),
    (9, 16, "R", "1.88%", "+0.94%"),
    (10, 10, "Delphi/Object Pascal", "1.80%", "-0.36%"),
    (11, 24, "Perl", "1.75%", "+1.05%"),
    (12, 12, "Scratch", "1.63%", "-0.03%"),
    (13, 11, "Fortran", "1.45%", "-0.25%"),
    (14, 14, "Rust", "1.31%", "+0.09%"),
    (15, 15, "MATLAB", "1.29%", "+0.31%"),
    (16, 7, "Go", "1.29%", "-1.49%"),
    (17, 17, "Assembly language", "1.29%", "+0.42%"),
    (18, 13, "PHP", "1.23%", "-0.25%"),
    (19, 18, "Ada", "1.10%", "+0.25%"),
    (20, 26, "Swift", "1.04%", "+0.44%"),
]

HALL_OF_FAME = [
    (2025, "C#"),
    (2024, "Python"),
    (2023, "C#"),
    (2022, "C++"),
    (2021, "Python"),
    (2020, "Python"),
    (2019, "C"),
    (2018, "Python"),
    (2016, "Go"),
]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helper functions
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def set_slide_bg(slide, color):
    background = slide.background
    fill = background.fill
    fill.solid()
    fill.fore_color.rgb = color


def add_text_box(slide, left, top, width, height, text, font_size=Pt(18),
                 bold=False, color=DARK_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT,
                 font_name="Calibri", valign=MSO_ANCHOR.TOP):
    txBox = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height)
    tf = txBox.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    tf.auto_size = None
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = text
    p.font.size = font_size
    p.font.bold = bold
    p.font.color.rgb = color
    p.font.name = font_name
    p.alignment = align
    tf.anchor = valign
    return txBox


def add_bullet_text(slide, left, top, width, height, bullets,
                    font_size=Pt(18), color=DARK_TEXT, font_name="Calibri",
                    line_spacing=1.2):
    txBox = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height)
    tf = txBox.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    tf.auto_size = None
    for i, bullet in enumerate(bullets):
        if i == 0:
            p = tf.paragraphs[0]
        else:
            p = tf.add_paragraph()
        p.text = bullet
        p.font.size = font_size
        p.font.color.rgb = color
        p.font.name = font_name
        p.level = 0
        p.space_after = Pt(8)
    return txBox


def style_table_header(table, color=PRIMARY):
    for cell in table.rows[0].cells:
        cell.fill.solid()
        cell.fill.fore_color.rgb = color
        para = cell.text_frame.paragraphs[0]
        para.font.color.rgb = WHITE
        para.font.bold = True
        para.font.size = Pt(11)
        para.alignment = PP_ALIGN.CENTER
        cell.text_frame.paragraphs[0].font.name = "Calibri"


def style_table_data(table, alternate=True):
    for i, row in enumerate(table.rows[1:], start=1):
        for cell in row.cells:
            if alternate and i % 2 == 0:
                cell.fill.solid()
                cell.fill.fore_color.rgb = LIGHT_BG
            para = cell.text_frame.paragraphs[0]
            para.font.size = Pt(10)
            para.font.name = "Calibri"
            para.alignment = PP_ALIGN.CENTER


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Create presentation
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

prs.slide_width = SLIDE_WIDTH
prs.slide_height = SLIDE_HEIGHT

# ===========================================================================
# Slide 1 — Title
# ===========================================================================

# Accent bar at top

    MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(0), Inches(0), SLIDE_WIDTH, Inches(0.15)
)
bar.fill.solid()
bar.fill.fore_color.rgb = PRIMARY
bar.line.fill.background()

# Title
add_text_box(slide1, MARGIN, Inches(2.2), Inches(12.333), Inches(1.2),
             "TIOBE Index March 2026: How 20+ Search Engines Rank the World's Programming Languages",
             font_size=Pt(40), bold=True, color=PRIMARY, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)

# Subtitle
add_text_box(slide1, MARGIN, Inches(3.5), Inches(12.333), Inches(0.8),
             "A Data-Backed Analysis of Programming Language Popularity Trends",
             font_size=Pt(24), bold=False, color=DARK_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)

# Metadata box
meta_box = slide1.shapes.add_shape(
    MSO_SHAPE.ROUNDED_RECTANGLE,
    Inches(3.5), Inches(4.6), Inches(6.333), Inches(1.4)
)
meta_box.fill.solid()
meta_box.fill.fore_color.rgb = LIGHT_BG
meta_box.line.color.rgb = SECONDARY

add_text_box(slide1, Inches(3.7), Inches(4.75), Inches(5.933), Inches(1.1),
             "Source: TIOBE Programming Community Index (tiobe.com)\n"
             "Methodology: Search-engine hit counts across Google, Bing, Wikipedia, Amazon, and 20+ sites\n"
             "Audience: Software Engineering Leads & Technology Strategists",
             font_size=Pt(14), color=DARK_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)

# ===========================================================================
# Slide 2 — Top 20 Rankings (table + bar chart)
# ===========================================================================
slide2 = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[6])
set_slide_bg(slide2, WHITE)

# Top accent bar
bar2 = slide2.shapes.add_shape(
    MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(0), Inches(0), SLIDE_WIDTH, Inches(0.08)
)
bar2.fill.solid()
bar2.fill.fore_color.rgb = PRIMARY
bar2.line.fill.background()

# Title
add_text_box(slide2, MARGIN, Inches(0.2), Inches(12.333), Inches(0.6),
             "Python Holds #1 at 21.25% but C Surges to #2 with the Largest Gain",
             font_size=Pt(28), bold=True, color=PRIMARY)

# Subtitle line
add_text_box(slide2, MARGIN, Inches(0.75), Inches(12.333), Inches(0.4),
             "Top 20 Programming Languages — March 2026 vs. March 2025",
             font_size=Pt(14), color=DARK_TEXT)

# Table
rows, cols = 21, 5
table_left = MARGIN
table_top = Inches(1.2)
table_width = Inches(7.5)
table_height = Inches(5.8)

table = slide2.shapes.add_table(rows, cols, table_left, table_top, table_width, table_height).table
table.columns[0].width = Inches(1.0)
table.columns[1].width = Inches(1.2)
table.columns[2].width = Inches(2.4)
table.columns[3].width = Inches(1.4)
table.columns[4].width = Inches(1.5)

headers = ["Rank 2026", "Rank 2025", "Language", "Rating", "YoY Change"]
for i, h in enumerate(headers):
    table.cell(0, i).text = h

for row_idx, data in enumerate(TOP20_DATA, start=1):
    rank_2026, rank_2025, lang, rating, yoy = data
    table.cell(row_idx, 0).text = str(rank_2026)
    table.cell(row_idx, 1).text = str(rank_2025)
    table.cell(row_idx, 2).text = lang
    table.cell(row_idx, 3).text = rating
    table.cell(row_idx, 4).text = yoy
    # Color YoY
    yoy_cell = table.cell(row_idx, 4)
    if yoy.startswith("+"):
        yoy_cell.text_frame.paragraphs[0].font.color.rgb = GREEN
